title: Algebra: equations and inequalities
lines: GRE algebra is high-school algebra done carefully. The questions are rarely long; they punish sign slips, dividing by a variable that might be zero, and forgetting to flip an inequality. Two strategies, plugging in numbers and back-solving, can replace algebra entirely when the algebra gets messy.
## Linear equations
- Do the same thing to both sides: clear fractions first (multiply by the common denominator), collect the variable on one side, then divide.
- Check by substituting your answer into the original equation.
> Multiply both sides by 2: 3x − 4 = 2x + 10.
> Subtract 2x and add 4: x = 14.
! Never divide both sides by a variable expression. From x² = 5x, dividing by x loses the solution x = 0. Instead write x² − 5x = 0, so x(x − 5) = 0 and x = 0 or x = 5.
## Systems of equations
- Substitution: solve one equation for a variable and put it into the other.
- Elimination: add or subtract the equations (after scaling) so a variable cancels.

- Two different linear equations in two unknowns usually have one solution. If one equation is a multiple of the other, there are infinitely many; if the left sides are multiples but the right sides are not, there are none.
- Read what is asked. Often the question wants x + y or x − y, which you can get in one step.
> Solve 2x + 3y = 12 and 5x − y = 13.
> From the second, y = 5x − 13. Substitute: 2x + 3(5x − 13) = 12, so 17x − 39 = 12 and x = 3.
> 3x + 2y = 17 and 2x + 3y = 13. Find x + y.
> Add the equations: 5x + 5y = 30, so x + y = 6.
> (Subtracting gives x − y = 4, so x = 5 and y = 1, but the question never needed them.)
## Inequalities
- Solve like equations, except: multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality sign.
- In QC and "must be true" questions, do not multiply both sides by a variable unless you know its sign.
- To combine ranges, find the extremes. For a − b, use the largest a with the smallest b and vice versa.
> Solve −3x + 5 > 17.
> −3x > 12. Divide by −3 and flip: x < −4.
> −2 < a < 3 and 1 < b < 4. What is the range of a − b?
> Largest: a near 3 and b near 1, so a − b < 2. Smallest: a near −2 and b near 4, so a − b > −6.
! Subtracting ranges end to end gives the wrong answer: (−2 − 1) to (3 − 4) is −3 to −1, which misses most of the true range.
## Inequalities with absolute value
- |x − c| ≤ k means x is within k of c: c − k ≤ x ≤ c + k.
- |x − c| > k means x is more than k from c: x < c − k or x > c + k (two separate pieces).
> Solve |x − 4| ≤ 3.
> x is within 3 of 4, so 1 ≤ x ≤ 7.
> Solve |3 − 2x| > 5.
> Case 1: 3 − 2x > 5 gives −2x > 2, so x < −1.
> Case 2: 3 − 2x < −5 gives −2x < −8, so x > 4.
> Solution: x < −1 or x > 4. Test x = 0: |3| = 3 is not greater than 5, so the middle is correctly excluded.
## Simplifying and factoring
- Distribute carefully: −(x − 3) = −x + 3.
- Common factor first: 6x² − 9x = 3x(2x − 3).
- Trinomials: x² + bx + c = (x + p)(x + q) where p + q = b and pq = c.
- The three identities to know on sight: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²; (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b²; a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b).
- Cancel factors, never terms: (x + 6)/6 is not x + 1.
> Simplify (x² − 9)/(x² + x − 6).
> Cancel (x + 3): the result is (x − 3)/(x − 2), for x ≠ −3 and x ≠ 2.
> x + y = 7 and xy = 10. Find x² + y².
> (x + y)² = x² + 2xy + y², so 49 = x² + y² + 20 and x² + y² = 29.
> Compute 99 × 101 without a calculator.
! (a + b)² is not a² + b². The GRE builds wrong answer choices from exactly this mistake.
## Symbolic manipulation
- To solve a formula for one letter, treat the other letters as numbers and undo operations in reverse order.
- If an expression is asked for (for example 4x − 6y), look for a multiple of a given expression before solving.
> Solve 1/x + 1/y = 1/z for z.
> Combine the left side: (y + x)/(xy) = 1/z.
> Take reciprocals: z = xy/(x + y).
> 2x − 3y = 5. What is 4x − 6y + 1?
> 4x − 6y = 2(2x − 3y) = 10, so the expression equals 11.
## Shortcuts: plug in numbers and back-solve

- Plug in when the answer choices contain variables. Choose easy, distinct numbers (avoid 0 and 1, which make different expressions look equal), compute a target, then test each choice. Check all five: more than one might match by chance.
- Back-solve when the choices are numbers and the question asks for a single value. Start with the middle choice; if it is too big, go smaller.
> Plug in: p pencils cost c cents. How many pencils can you buy for d dollars?
> Let p = 2, c = 50, d = 1. Two pencils cost 50 cents, so $1 buys 4 pencils.
> Test the choice 100dp/c: 100 × 1 × 2 / 50 = 4. It matches; a choice like dp/(100c) gives 0.0004 and fails.
> Back-solve: a number plus half of it plus a third of it equals 66. Choices: 30, 33, 36, 40, 44.
> Try 36: 36 + 18 + 12 = 66. Done in one step.
! When you plug in, confirm the numbers satisfy every condition in the question (for example "x > y" or "n is odd").
## QC with algebra
- Simplify both quantities the same way, but only add, subtract, or multiply and divide by known positives.
- If an equation has two solutions (a quadratic or an absolute value), test both: the answer is often "cannot be determined".
> x² = 5x. Quantity A: x. Quantity B: 3.
> x = 0 makes B greater; x = 5 makes A greater. The relationship cannot be determined.
## Timing
- If setting up an equation takes more than 30 seconds, switch to back-solving or plugging in.
- Use the on-screen calculator for arithmetic inside a solved equation, never to guess and check a system blindly.
